hook: Type a sentence. *Walk* into a world.
dek: Google DeepMind's Genie 4 builds explorable scenes with sound and talking characters from a single prompt.

slides.label: The drop
slides.text: Last Tuesday, Oct. 27, Google DeepMind unveiled *Genie 4*, a world model that turns a text prompt into a place you can *walk through* with a keyboard. It is a research preview, not a product.

slides.label: How it works
slides.text: Describe a scene and Genie 4 generates it *frame by frame in real time*. Mid-session, type changes like weather, a camera angle or a new person walking in. The world adjusts *without starting over*.

slides.label: The sound
slides.text: The headline upgrade is audio: ambient sound, music and characters who *talk back*. Google calls it the first real-time world model with native audio, but Runway's *GWM Worlds 2* also generates audio.

slides.label: The limits
slides.text: TechCrunch reported scenes hold together for about *two minutes*. Details drift and objects vanish, and text, physics and audio remain unsolved. DataCamp: *"Treat the demo audio as a ceiling rather than a floor."*

slides.label: Who gets it
slides.text: Only *trusted testers* for now. Google AI Ultra subscribers come next, then Gemini API partners. No public price, no release date. Every frame carries *SynthID* watermarking, not yet independently validated.

slides.label: The upside
slides.text: Testers are running live film takes, turning *archival photos* into explorable spaces and prototyping games before writing engine code. For a director with *no location budget*, that changes who gets a meeting.

slides.label: The other side
slides.text: Bloomberg framed Genie 4 as rattling *video game stocks*. Prototyping, concept art and previsualization look most exposed, and those jobs have been *entry points* for young Black and Brown creatives.

slides.label: The Den's take
slides.text: Genie 4 drifts, forgets and cannot write a readable sign. But the direction is clear. Get close to world models early, learn the vocabulary, and *be in the room* when access opens.

Type a sentence, get a place. Not a picture or a clip, a world you can walk through.

Google DeepMind unveiled Genie 4 on Oct. 27. You describe a scene, it generates it in real time, and you move through it with a keyboard while typing changes like rain or a new character. It adds ambient sound, music and characters who talk back. TechCrunch reported scenes stay consistent for about two minutes. Only trusted testers have it now, with Google AI Ultra subscribers next, and every frame carries SynthID watermarking.

The other side: Google's "first" audio claim is contested, since Runway's GWM Worlds 2 also generates audio. Details drift, objects vanish, and Bloomberg framed the news as rattling video game stocks. Prototyping and concept art, entry points for a lot of young creatives, look most exposed.
